chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: Outwardly, Pierre had barely changed at all. He looked the same as he always had. He was still absent-minded and seemed occupied not with what was in front of him but with something of his own. The difference between the old Pierre and the new was this: before, when he failed to grasp what was before him or what was being said, he would furrow his brow painfully, as if straining to make out something in the distance. Now he still forgot what people said to him and still didn't see what was right before his eyes, but he looked at everything with a barely perceptible, seemingly ironic smile, and listened to what was said while clearly seeing and hearing something entirely different. Before, he had seemed like a kindhearted but unhappy man, and people had tended to avoid him. Now a smile of pure joy played constantly around his lips, and his eyes shone with sympathy for others and a quiet question: were they as happy as he was? People felt genuinely pleased to be around him.

Before, he had talked a lot, got excited when he spoke, and rarely listened. Now he seldom got carried away in conversation and knew how to listen in a way that made people readily share their most intimate secrets with him.

The princess, who had never liked Pierre and had been especially hostile toward him since feeling indebted to him after the old count's death, had now—after staying a short time in Orel, where she had come intending to show Pierre that despite his ingratitude she felt duty-bound to nurse him—found to her surprise and irritation that she had grown fond of him. Pierre made no effort to win her approval; he simply studied her with interest. Before, she had felt that he looked at her with indifference and irony, so she had retreated into herself as she did with everyone, showing him only her combative side. But now he seemed to be reaching for the most hidden places in her heart, and—mistrustfully at first, then gratefully—she let him see the kind, gentle sides of her nature.

The most cunning person in the world couldn't have won her trust more effectively, drawing out memories of the best times of her youth and showing sympathy for them. Yet Pierre's cunning consisted simply in the pleasure he took in bringing out the human qualities of this bitter, hardened, and—in her own way—proud princess.
"Yes, he's a very, very kind man when he's not under the influence of bad people but of people like me," she thought.

His servants too—Terenty and Vaska—noticed the change in Pierre in their own way. They thought he had become much "simpler." Terenty, after helping him undress and wishing him good night, would often linger with his master's boots in his hands and clothes over his arm, hoping Pierre might start a conversation. And Pierre, noticing that Terenty wanted to chat, usually kept him there.
"Well, tell me—how did you manage to get food?" he would ask.

And Terenty would start talking about the destruction of Moscow and the old count, standing there a long time holding the clothes and talking, or sometimes listening to Pierre's stories, before going out to the hall with a pleasant feeling of closeness to his master and genuine affection for him.

The doctor who attended Pierre and visited him every day—though he felt obligated to act as if his every moment were precious to suffering humanity—would sit for hours with Pierre, telling his favorite stories and sharing observations about his patients' characters, especially the ladies.
"It's a pleasure to talk to a man like that; he's nothing like our provincial types," he would say.
There were several French prisoners of war in Orel, and the doctor brought one of them, a young Italian, to meet Pierre.
This officer began visiting Pierre regularly, and the princess liked to tease him about the Italian's open affection.
The Italian seemed happy only when he could visit Pierre, talk with him, tell him about his past life back home and his love, and pour out his outrage against the French and especially Napoleon.
"If all Russians are anything like you, it's a sin to fight such a nation," he told Pierre. "You, who suffered so much from the French, don't even feel any resentment toward them."
Pierre had won the Italian's passionate devotion simply by drawing out the best in him and taking pleasure in doing so.

During Pierre's last days in Orel, his old Masonic acquaintance Count Willarski—who had introduced him to the lodge back in 1807—came to see him. Willarski had married a Russian heiress with a large estate in Orel province and held a temporary post in the local commissariat department.

Hearing that Bezukhov was in Orel, Willarski—though they had never been close—came to him with the kind of warm declarations of friendship that people who meet in a desert tend to exchange. Willarski was bored in Orel and was glad to meet someone from his own circle who, he assumed, shared his interests.
But to his surprise, Willarski quickly noticed that Pierre had fallen far behind the times and had sunk, as he put it to himself, into apathy and self-absorption.
"You're letting yourself go, my dear fellow," he said.

But despite all that, Willarski found it more pleasant than before to spend time with Pierre, and came to see him every day. To Pierre, as he watched and listened to Willarski, it seemed strange to think that he himself had been just like that not so long ago.

Willarski was a married man with a family, busy with his family affairs, his wife's affairs, and his official duties. He saw all these occupations as obstacles to real life, and considered them contemptible because their aim was merely the welfare of himself and his family. Military, administrative, political, and Masonic concerns constantly consumed his attention. And Pierre, without trying to change his views or condemning him, but with the calm, joyful, and amused smile that was now habitual, watched this strange yet very familiar phenomenon with interest.

There was something new in Pierre's dealings with Willarski, with the princess, with the doctor, and with everyone he met—something that earned him universal goodwill. It was his acceptance of the impossibility of changing anyone's mind through words, and his recognition that everyone thinks, feels, and sees things from their own perspective. This natural uniqueness of each person, which used to excite and irritate Pierre, now became the basis for the sympathy he felt and the interest he took in other people. The differences—and sometimes outright contradictions—between what people believed and how they lived, and between one person and another, pleased him and drew from him an amused, gentle smile.

In practical matters, Pierre unexpectedly discovered a sense of inner balance he had never had before. Previously, all financial questions—especially requests for money, to which he was constantly exposed as an extremely wealthy man—had thrown him into a state of helpless anxiety and confusion. "Should I give or not?" he would ask himself. "I have it and he needs it. But someone else needs it more. Who needs it most? And maybe they're both frauds?" In the old days he had found no way out of such dilemmas and had given to everyone who asked, as long as he had anything left to give. He had been in a similar state of paralysis regarding every question about his property, when one adviser said one thing and another said the opposite.

Now, to his surprise, he found that he no longer felt any doubt or confusion about these things. There was now a judge inside him who, by some rule Pierre couldn't identify, decided what should and shouldn't be done.

He was as indifferent to money as ever, but now he felt certain about what was right and what wasn't. The first time he relied on this new inner judge was when a French prisoner, a colonel, came to him and—after talking at length about his military exploits—essentially demanded that Pierre give him four thousand francs to send to his wife and children. Pierre refused without the slightest difficulty or effort, and was amazed afterward at how simple and easy something had been that once seemed impossibly hard. At the same time that he refused the colonel, he decided he would need to find a tactful way, when leaving Orel, to get the Italian officer to accept some money he clearly needed. Another sign of Pierre's more settled practical judgment was his decision about his wife's debts and the rebuilding of his houses in and near Moscow.
His head steward came to see him in Orel, and Pierre went over his reduced income with him. According to the steward's calculations, the burning of Moscow had cost Pierre about two million rubles.

To comfort Pierre for these losses, the steward presented an estimate showing that despite everything, his income would actually increase—if he refused to pay his wife's debts, which he was under no legal obligation to pay, and didn't rebuild his Moscow house or the country estate nearby, which had cost eighty thousand rubles a year and brought in nothing.
"Yes, of course, that's true," Pierre said with a cheerful smile. "I don't need any of that at all. By being ruined, I've become much richer."

But in January, Savelich arrived from Moscow with an account of the situation there, including an architect's estimate for rebuilding the town house and country house, speaking of it as a settled matter. Around the same time, Pierre received letters from Prince Vasili and other Petersburg acquaintances about his wife's debts. And Pierre decided that the steward's proposals, which had pleased him so much, were wrong—that he needed to go to Petersburg to settle his wife's affairs, and he needed to rebuild in Moscow. Why this was necessary he couldn't say, but he knew with certainty that it had to be done. His income would be cut by three-quarters, but he felt it was right.
Willarski was heading to Moscow, and they agreed to travel together.

Throughout his recovery in Orel, Pierre had felt a sense of joy, freedom, and life; but during his journey, surrounded by the open world and hundreds of new faces, that feeling only intensified. He felt like a schoolboy on holiday. Everyone—the coach driver, the post-house overseers, the peasants on the roads and in the villages—held a fresh significance for him. Willarski's constant complaints about the ignorance and poverty of Russia and its backwardness compared to Europe only heightened Pierre's delight. Where Willarski saw stagnation, Pierre saw extraordinary strength and vitality—the strength that sustained the life of this original, distinctive, and unique people across those vast, snow-covered spaces. He didn't argue with Willarski and even seemed to agree with him—since apparent agreement was the simplest way to avoid pointless debates—and he smiled joyfully as he listened.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: It would be hard to explain why and where ants rush when their anthill has been destroyed: some hauling away bits of debris, larvae, and dead bodies, others streaming back to the hill, or why they bump into each other, chase one another, and fight. But it would be equally hard to explain what drove people to swarm back to Moscow after the French had gone. And just as when you watch ants around their ruined hill, despite the complete destruction of the colony the tenacity, energy, and sheer number of the swarming insects show that everything has been destroyed except something indestructible and immaterial—the spirit of the colony—so too Moscow in October, despite the absence of any authorities, churches, treasures, or houses, was still the same Moscow it had been in August. Everything was destroyed except something intangible yet powerful and indestructible.

The motives of those who flooded into Moscow from all directions were enormously varied and personal, and at first mostly savage and brutal. Only one motive was shared by all: the pull toward the place that had once been called Moscow, to apply their energies there.
Within a week Moscow had fifteen thousand inhabitants; in two weeks, twenty-five thousand; and so on, rising steadily. By autumn 1813 the population exceeded what it had been before 1812.

The first Russians to enter Moscow were the Cossacks of Wintzingerode's detachment, peasants from nearby villages, and residents who had fled Moscow and been hiding in the surrounding area. The Russians who returned to Moscow, finding it plundered, began plundering it themselves. They continued what the French had started. Peasant cart-drivers came from all around to steal the goods scattered throughout Moscow's ruined neighborhoods. Cossacks carried off whatever they could to their camps; homeowners took everything they found in other people's houses and moved it into their own, claiming it as their property.
But the first wave of plunderers was followed by a second and a third, and as numbers grew, the plundering became harder and took on more definite forms.

The French had found Moscow abandoned but with all the systems of an organized society intact—diverse branches of commerce and craftsmanship, luxury goods, government offices, and religious institutions. These forms were lifeless but still existed. There were markets, shops, warehouses, grain stores, and bazaars—most of them still stocked with goods. There were factories and workshops. There were palaces and wealthy mansions filled with luxury items. There were hospitals, prisons, government buildings, churches, and cathedrals. The longer the French stayed, the more these forms of city life crumbled away, and at the end nothing was left but mindless, purposeless plundering.

The longer the French plundering continued, the more both Moscow's wealth and the plunderers' strength were destroyed. But the Russian plundering that accompanied the reoccupation of the capital—since it was carried out by such vast numbers and was directed at what still remained—quickly brought Moscow back to life. And just as water seeping into a dry sponge does not flow freely anymore, neither separately nor as a pool, so the army and population flooding into Moscow simply spread through the ruined city, which soaked them up, and the process of restoration began.

Besides the plunderers, all sorts of people—some drawn by curiosity, some by official duties, some by self-interest—homeowners, clergy, officials of every kind, tradesmen, artisans, and peasants—streamed into Moscow from every direction, like blood rushing to the heart.

Within a week, the peasants who had come with empty carts to haul away plunder were stopped by the authorities and forced to cart dead bodies out of the city instead. Other peasants, hearing what had happened to their neighbors, brought in cartloads of grain, hay, and charcoal, undercutting each other's prices until they fell below what they had been before. Crews of carpenters hoping for high wages arrived daily, and on all sides new houses were going up and burned ones were being repaired. Merchants set up shop in makeshift stalls. Restaurants and inns opened in fire-damaged buildings. The clergy resumed services in many of the churches that had escaped the fire. Donors contributed looted church furnishings that had been recovered. Officials set up their small offices with writing desks and filing cabinets in small rooms. The higher authorities and the police organized the distribution of goods left behind by the French. The owners of houses in which a great deal of property from other buildings had been gathered complained of the unfairness of having everything taken to the Faceted Palace, while others argued that the French had brought things from different houses to one location, and it was therefore unfair to let the owner of that house keep everything found in it. People cursed the police and bribed them; estimates for the rebuilding of government buildings were drawn up ten times their real cost; and appeals for help were made. The old count's Rostov spirit was alive, regenerating the city.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: At the end of January, Pierre arrived in Moscow and stayed in a wing of his house that hadn't been burned. He called on Count Rostopchin and some acquaintances who had returned, and planned to leave for Petersburg in two days. Everyone was celebrating the victory; the ruined capital was buzzing with life and energy. Pierre was welcomed everywhere; everyone wanted to see him and hear about what he'd been through. He felt warmly disposed toward all the people he met, but was now instinctively on guard with everyone, careful not to tie himself down in any way. To every question put to him—whether important or trivial—such as: Where would he live? Would he rebuild? When was he going to Petersburg? Could he deliver a certain parcel?—he would answer: "Yes, perhaps," or "I think so," and so on.

He had heard that the Rostovs were in Kostroma, but thoughts of Natasha rarely came to him. When they did, it was only as a pleasant memory of the distant past. He felt free not only from social obligations but from the feeling that he had chosen to impose on himself.

On the third day after his arrival, he learned from the Drubetskoys that Princess Mary was in Moscow. The death, suffering, and final days of Prince Andrew had often occupied Pierre's thoughts and now came back to him with fresh vividness. Having heard over dinner that Princess Mary was in Moscow and living in her own house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived the fire, he went to see her that same evening.
On his way to the house, Pierre kept thinking about Prince Andrew, about their friendship, their various meetings, and especially their last one at Borodino.

"Is it possible that he died in that bitter state of mind? Is it possible the meaning of life was never revealed to him before he died?" Pierre wondered. He thought of Karataev and his death, and involuntarily began comparing the two men—so different, yet somehow alike because of the love Pierre had felt for both and because both had lived and both had died.

Pierre drove up to the old prince's house in a very serious mood. The house had survived the fire; it showed signs of damage but its general appearance was unchanged. The old footman who greeted Pierre wore a stern expression, as if wanting to make the visitor feel that the absence of the old prince had not disrupted the household routine. He told Pierre that the princess had retired to her rooms and received visitors on Sundays.
"Please announce me. Perhaps she'll see me," said Pierre.
"Yes, sir," the man replied. "Please step into the portrait gallery."

A few minutes later the footman returned with Dessalles, who brought word from the princess that she would be very glad to see Pierre if he would excuse the informality and come upstairs to her rooms.

In a rather low room lit by a single candle sat the princess, and with her another person dressed in black. Pierre remembered that the princess always had lady companions, but who they were and what they were like he never knew. "This must be one of her companions," he thought, glancing at the woman in black.
The princess rose quickly to meet him and held out her hand.

"Yes," she said, looking at his changed face after he had kissed her hand, "so this is how we meet again. He spoke of you even at the very end," she went on, turning her eyes from Pierre to her companion with a shyness that surprised him.
"I was so glad to hear you were safe. It was the first good news we'd received in a long time."
Again the princess glanced at her companion with even more unease and was about to add something, but Pierre interrupted her.

"Imagine—I knew nothing about him!" he said. "I thought he'd been killed. Everything I know I heard secondhand from others. I only know that he ended up with the Rostovs... What a strange coincidence!"

Pierre spoke quickly and with animation. He glanced once at the companion's face, saw her attentive, kindly gaze fixed on him, and—as often happens when you're talking—felt somehow that this companion in the black dress was a good, kind, wonderful person who wouldn't interfere with his heartfelt conversation with Princess Mary.
But when he mentioned the Rostovs, Princess Mary's face showed still greater embarrassment. She again glanced rapidly from Pierre's face to that of the woman in the black dress and said:
"Don't you really recognize her?"

Pierre looked again at the companion's pale, delicate face with its dark eyes and distinctive mouth, and something near to him, long forgotten and more than sweet, looked back at him from those attentive eyes.

"But no, it can't be!" he thought. "This stern, thin, pale face that looks so much older! It can't be her. It just reminds me of her." But at that moment Princess Mary said, "Natasha!" And with difficulty, with effort, like a rusty door being forced open, a smile appeared on the face with the attentive eyes, and through that opening door came a fragrance from a long-forgotten world of happiness that Pierre had lost all thought of—especially now. It breathed over him, engulfed him, and swallowed him whole. When she smiled, there could be no doubt: it was Natasha, and he loved her.

In that moment, Pierre involuntarily revealed—to her, to Princess Mary, and above all to himself—a secret he hadn't even known he carried. He flushed with joy and painful emotion. He tried to hide his feelings. But the more he tried, the more clearly—more clearly than any words could have conveyed—he revealed to himself, to her, and to Princess Mary that he loved her.

"No, it's just the surprise," Pierre thought. But as soon as he tried to resume the conversation he'd been having with Princess Mary, he glanced again at Natasha, and a deeper flush spread across his face, and an even stronger wave of joy and agitation seized his heart.

Pierre had failed to notice Natasha because he hadn't expected to see her there, but he had failed to recognize her because the change in her since he'd last seen her was enormous. She had grown thin and pale. But it wasn't the thinness and pallor that made her unrecognizable—she was unrecognizable in the first moment because on that face, whose eyes had always shone with suppressed delight in life, there was now—when he first entered and glanced at her—not the slightest shadow of a smile. There were only eyes, watchful, kind, and sadly questioning.
Pierre's confusion was not mirrored by any confusion on Natasha's part—only by the pleasure that softly lit up her whole face.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: "She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a terrible state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They made her come with me."
"Yes, is there a single family untouched by grief right now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and by way of answer her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say or think of as consolation?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did such a splendid boy, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, in these times it would be hard to live without faith..." remarked Princess Mary.
"Yes, yes, that's absolutely true," Pierre quickly agreed.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking intently into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what awaits us—"
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked inquiringly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre continued, "only someone who believes that God is watching over us can bear a loss like hers and... yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to speak but suddenly stopped. Pierre quickly turned away from her and addressed Princess Mary again, asking about his friend's last days.

Pierre's confusion had now almost vanished, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had completely disappeared. He felt there was now a judge of his every word and action whose judgment mattered to him more than the judgment of all the rest of the world. As he spoke he was constantly aware of the impression his words were making on Natasha. He didn't deliberately say things to please her, but whatever he said, he judged himself through her eyes.

Princess Mary—with the reluctance usual in such cases—began describing the state in which she had found Prince Andrew. But Pierre's face, quivering with emotion, his questions and eager, restless expression, gradually compelled her to go into details she shrank from calling up in her own mind.

"Yes, yes, and so...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening intently. "Yes, yes... so he found peace and grew gentle? He had always sought one thing with all his soul—to be completely good—so he couldn't have been afraid of death. His flaws—if he had any—didn't come from within himself. So he did find peace?" Pierre asked. "What a blessing that he saw you again!" he added to Natasha.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated briefly over whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said in her quiet, deep voice. "For me it certainly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he said he was hoping for exactly that at the moment I came to see him..." Her voice broke.
Natasha blushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, and then, with a visible effort to control herself, lifted her head and began speaking rapidly.

"We knew nothing when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be near him," she said, trembling with agitation.
And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell what she had never told anyone—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of their journey and time in Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened with parted lips and eyes brimming with tears. As he listened, he thought not of Prince Andrew or of death, not of what she was telling him. He listened to her and felt nothing but compassion for the suffering she was going through now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning in her effort to hold back tears, sat beside Natasha and heard for the first time the story of those last days of her brother's love and Natasha's.
Clearly, Natasha needed to tell this painful yet somehow joyful story.
She spoke, weaving the most trivial details together with the deepest secrets of her soul, and it seemed she could never finish. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice was heard outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas might come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all—everything," said Natasha.
She jumped up quickly, almost ran to the door hidden behind curtains, bumped her head against it, and rushed from the room with a moan of either pain or grief.
Pierre gazed at the door through which she'd disappeared and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt completely alone in the world.
Princess Mary roused him from his thoughts by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

At that moment of emotional tenderness, young Nicholas's face—so like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy, he quickly stood up, pulled out his handkerchief, and walked to the window.
"No, Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought. Go downstairs—we'll be right there."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's spoken about him like that."

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: Pierre was shown into the large, brightly lit dining room. A few minutes later he heard footsteps, and Princess Mary entered with Natasha. Natasha was calm, though a serious, solemn expression had settled on her face again. Princess Mary, Natasha, and Pierre all equally felt that awkwardness that usually follows a serious and deeply felt conversation. To continue from where you left off is impossible; to talk about trivial things feels wrong; yet to sit in silence is unpleasant, because you want to be talking and this silence feels like pretending. They went to the table in silence. The servants pulled back their chairs and pushed them in. Pierre unfolded his cold napkin and, deciding to break the silence, glanced at Natasha and Princess Mary. Both had clearly reached the same decision at the same moment: in both their eyes shone satisfaction with life and an acknowledgment that besides grief there is also joy.
"Do you drink vodka, Count?" asked Princess Mary, and those words instantly banished the shadows of the past. "Now tell us about yourself," she said. "We hear such incredible stories about you."

"Yes," Pierre replied with the smile of mild irony that had become habitual. "People even tell me about wonders I never dreamed of! Maria Abramovna invited me over and kept telling me what had happened to me, or what should have happened. Stepan Stepanych also taught me how I ought to tell my story. In general, I've noticed that being an interesting person is very convenient"—he smiled at Natasha—"because people invite me out and then tell me everything themselves."
Natasha smiled and was about to speak.
"We've been told," Princess Mary interrupted, "that you lost two million rubles in Moscow. Is that true?"
"But I'm three times richer than before," Pierre replied.
Though his financial position had actually worsened—he'd decided to pay his wife's debts and rebuild his houses—Pierre still maintained that he was three times richer than before.
"What I've definitely gained is freedom," he began seriously, but stopped, sensing this was too self-centered a topic.
"And are you rebuilding?"
"Yes. Savelich says I have to!"

"Tell me—you didn't know about the countess's death when you decided to stay in Moscow?" asked Princess Mary, and immediately blushed, realizing that her question, coming right after his mention of freedom, seemed to attribute motives to him that perhaps he didn't deserve.

"No," Pierre answered, clearly not finding the implied meaning of Princess Mary's words at all awkward. "I heard about it in Orel, and you can't imagine how it shook me. We weren't a model couple," he said quickly, glancing at Natasha and sensing in her curious look a question about what his attitude toward his wife had been. "But that death hit me terribly hard. When two people quarrel, both are always at fault, and your own guilt suddenly becomes unbearably heavy when the other person is no longer alive. And then, such a death... without friends, without comfort. I felt very, very sorry for her," he finished, and was pleased to notice an expression of glad approval on Natasha's face.
"Yes, and so you're an eligible bachelor again," said Princess Mary.
Pierre suddenly flushed crimson and for a long time tried not to look at Natasha. When he ventured a glance her way, her face was cold, stern, and—he thought—even contemptuous.
"And did you really see and speak to Napoleon, as we've been told?" asked Princess Mary.
Pierre laughed.
"No, not once! Everyone seems to think that being a prisoner of war means being Napoleon's guest. I not only never saw him, I never even heard anything about him—I was in much lower company!"
Supper was over, and Pierre, who had at first declined to talk about his captivity, was gradually drawn into doing so.
"But is it true that you stayed in Moscow to kill Napoleon?" Natasha asked with a slight smile. "I guessed it back then, when we met at the Sukharev Tower. Do you remember?"
Pierre admitted it was true, and from there Princess Mary's questions and especially Natasha's gradually led him into giving a detailed account of his adventures.

At first he spoke with the amused, gentle irony that had become his usual manner toward everyone and especially toward himself. But when he came to the horrors and sufferings he'd witnessed, he was carried away without realizing it and began speaking with the restrained emotion of someone reliving painful memories.

Princess Mary looked from Pierre to Natasha with a gentle smile. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly changing with the story, watched Pierre without taking her eyes off him for a single moment, clearly living through everything he described along with him.
"You're not telling us everything—I'm sure you did something..." Natasha said, then paused and added, "something fine?"
Pierre continued. When he reached the execution, he tried to skip over the horrible details, but Natasha insisted that he leave nothing out.
Pierre began to speak about Karataev, then stopped. By this time he had risen from the table and was pacing the room, Natasha following him with her eyes. Then he added:
"No, you can't understand what I learned from that uneducated man—that simple fellow."
"Yes, yes, go on!" said Natasha. "Where is he?"
"They killed him almost before my eyes."
And Pierre, his voice trembling the whole time, went on to tell about the last days of their retreat, Karataev's illness, and his death.

He told his story as he had never recalled it before. He now seemed to see a new meaning in everything he'd been through. And now, telling it all to Natasha, he experienced that pleasure a man feels when women listen to him—not clever women who, when they listen, try to either memorize what they hear in order to enrich their own minds and then repeat it, or to fit what they're told into their own framework and contribute their own clever comments worked out in their own little mental world—but the pleasure that comes from real women, gifted with the ability to select and absorb all that is best in what a man reveals of himself. Natasha, without knowing it, was all attention: she didn't miss a word, a tremor in his voice, a glance, a twitch of his facial muscles, or a gesture. She caught each word on the fly and carried it straight to her open heart, intuiting the mysterious meaning of Pierre's entire spiritual journey.

Princess Mary understood his story and felt for him, but she saw something else now that absorbed all her attention. She saw the possibility of love and happiness between Natasha and Pierre, and this thought, occurring to her for the first time, filled her heart with joy.
It was three in the morning. The servants came in with sad, stern faces to change the candles, but nobody noticed them.

Pierre finished his story. Natasha continued to look at him intently with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as if trying to understand something more that he had perhaps left untold. Pierre, in shy, happy confusion, kept glancing at her and trying to think of something to say that might shift the conversation to a different subject. He began speaking, and Princess Mary too looked at Natasha. She had often been near a woman in love and had seen that look before; she recognized it now on Natasha's face, and she understood.

"People talk about misfortunes and suffering," Pierre said, "but if right now someone asked me, 'Would you rather be what you were before you were taken prisoner, or go through it all again?'—for God's sake, let me go through captivity again and eat horseflesh! We imagine that the moment we're knocked out of our usual track, everything is lost. But that's just when something new and good begins. As long as there's life, there's happiness. There's a great deal, a great deal ahead of us. I'm saying this to you," he added, turning to Natasha.
"Yes, yes," she said, answering something quite different. "I too would wish for nothing but to live it all over from the beginning."
Pierre looked at her intently.
"Yes, and nothing more," said Natasha.
"It's not true, not true!" Pierre cried. "I'm not to blame for being alive and wanting to live—and neither are you!"
Suddenly Natasha bent her head, covered her face with her hands, and began to cry.
"What is it, Natasha?" said Princess Mary.
"Nothing, nothing." She smiled at Pierre through her tears. "Good night! It's time for bed."
Pierre got up and said goodbye.
Princess Mary and Natasha met as usual in the bedroom. They talked about what Pierre had told them. Princess Mary didn't say what she thought of Pierre, and Natasha didn't mention him either.
"Well, good night, Mary!" said Natasha. "Do you know, I'm often afraid that by not talking about him"—she meant Prince Andrew—"for fear of not doing justice to our feelings, we're forgetting him."
Princess Mary sighed deeply, acknowledging the justice of Natasha's remark, but didn't say so in words.
"Is it possible to forget?" she said.

"It did me so much good to tell everything today. It was hard and painful, but good—very good!" said Natasha. "I'm sure he truly loved him. That's why I told him... Was it all right?" she added, suddenly blushing.
"You mean telling Pierre? Oh yes. What a wonderful man he is!" said Princess Mary.

"Do you know, Mary..." Natasha suddenly said with a mischievous smile—the kind Princess Mary hadn't seen on her face for a long time—"he's somehow grown so clean, smooth, and fresh—as if he'd just come out of a bath. Don't you think? Out of a moral bath. Right?"
"Yes," Princess Mary replied. "He's improved enormously."
"With a short coat and his hair cropped; just as if—well, just as if he'd come straight from the bath... Papa used to—"
"I understand why he"—meaning Prince Andrew—"loved no one so much as him," said Princess Mary.
"Yes, and yet he's completely different from him. People say men become friends when they're very different. That must be true. He really is nothing like him—in anything."
"Yes, but he's wonderful."
"Well, good night," said Natasha.
And the same mischievous smile lingered on her face for a long time, as if it had been forgotten there.
